title: ILP Fundamentals
summary: What limits how many instructions a CPU can run per cycle from a single stream, and the three dependence types every ILP technique works around.

slides.markdown:
**Instruction-level parallelism (ILP)** is how many instructions from one sequential program a CPU executes per cycle instead of one at a time. A pipeline already completes one instruction per cycle at best ([classic-5-stage-pipeline](classic-5-stage-pipeline)); ILP techniques push past that.

The catch: the program is still one ordered stream. Every ILP technique — superscalar, out-of-order, VLIW — answers one question: **which instructions here are independent enough to run together?** That means naming the ways two instructions *can't* be reordered.

A **true data dependence** (read-after-write, RAW) is the one limiter that never goes away: instruction B genuinely needs a value instruction A produces.

```
ADD R1, R2, R3   ; A writes R1
SUB R4, R1, R5   ; B reads R1
```

No amount of cleverness lets B use R1 before A computes it — you can only shrink the *wait*, via forwarding ([data-hazards-and-forwarding](data-hazards-and-forwarding)) or by finding other independent work to fill the gap. RAW is why real programs never reach their theoretical peak ILP: the true dependence chain sets a hard floor on execution time.

**WAR** (write-after-read) and **WAW** (write-after-write) aren't about data flowing between instructions at all — they're **name dependences**: two unrelated instructions happen to reuse the same register name.

```
SUB R4, R1, R5   ; A reads R1
ADD R1, R6, R7   ; B writes R1 (unrelated value!)
```

If B's write happened before A's read, A would get the wrong value — but only because they share the label `R1`, not because B's result depends on A. Give B a different register and the hazard vanishes entirely. That's exactly what **register renaming** exploits ([register-renaming](register-renaming)) to unlock reordering that RAW alone would never allow.

A **control dependence** ties an instruction's execution to a branch outcome: `SUB R4, R1, R5` inside an `if` block only truly executes if the branch is taken. The hardware doesn't know which path is real until the branch resolves — yet stalling every instruction after a branch until then would gut throughput.

The practical answer is **branch prediction** ([branch-prediction](branch-prediction)): guess the direction, execute speculatively past it, and roll back on a misprediction. Control dependence is the reason ILP techniques need a *recovery* mechanism, not just a *scheduling* one.

slides.sectionTitle: Seeing it on a dependence graph
slides.markdown:
A **dependence graph** makes parallelism visible: independent instructions have no edge and can run the same cycle; chained ones must run in order.

![A dependence graph for four instructions, marking a RAW chain and one independent instruction](assets/dependence-graph.svg)

1→2→4 form a RAW chain; instruction 3 depends on nothing — runs alongside 1 or 2. The **longest chain**, not instruction count, bounds execution time.

assets.alt: A dependence graph for four instructions, marking a RAW chain and one independent instruction

slides.markdown:
Each dependence type has a distinct fix — mixing them up is a common interview stumble.

| Dependence | Real constraint? | Fixed by |
|---|---|---|
| RAW (true) | Yes — value must flow | Forwarding/bypassing |
| WAR / WAW (name) | No — just reused names | Register renaming |
| Control | Yes — outcome unknown yet | Branch prediction + speculation |

**How to decide which applies:** ask whether the second instruction needs a *value* from the first (RAW), merely reuses its *register name* (WAR/WAW), or waits on a *branch outcome* (control) — the answer picks the technique.
